hints: Think about oxidation numbers. Copper changes from +2 to +1 in the precipitate, so iodide must be oxidised to iodine at the same time.
walkthrough:
Sort out what is oxidised and what is reduced**
Picture the products. You make solid $\text{CuI}$ where copper is $+1$, so $\text{Cu}^{2+}$ has gained an electron and been reduced. The other product is $\text{I}_{2}$, so $\text{I}^{-}$ has lost electrons and been oxidised.

Balance electrons and atoms**
Each $\text{Cu}^{2+}$ needs one electron to become $\text{Cu}^{+}$, and two $\text{I}^{-}$ lose two electrons to make one $\text{I}_{2}$. To balance the two electrons lost, you need two $\text{Cu}^{2+}$ reduced. That gives $$2\text{Cu}^{2+} + 4\text{I}^{-} \rightarrow 2\text{CuI} + \text{I}_{2}$$ with atoms and charge balanced.

hints: Remember copper(II) in water exists as a complex ion, $\text{[Cu(H}_{2}\text{O)}_{6}\text{]}^{2+}$. Think about what water ligands do to the energies of the five 3d orbitals.
Recall that electrons can move between these split d orbitals if they absorb just the right amount of energy.
Think about where that energy comes from, and what happens to white light when one wavelength is removed.
Link the colour you actually see to the light that is left over after absorption.
walkthrough:
Start with splitting, not just d electrons**
In solution you do not have bare $\text{Cu}^{2+}$. You have the blue complex $\text{[Cu(H}_{2}\text{O)}_{6}\text{]}^{2+}$. The six water ligands approach along the axes and repel the d electrons unevenly, so the five 3d orbitals are no longer equal in energy. They split into a lower set and a higher set with a small energy gap.

Use light to jump the gap**
$\text{Cu}^{2+}$ is $3\text{d}^{9}$, so there is a vacancy in the upper level. An electron from the lower 3d level can absorb exactly the energy of the gap and get promoted to the upper level. This is a d-d transition.

See where the energy comes from**
That energy is supplied by visible light. When white light shines through the solution, one particular wavelength / frequency corresponding to $$\Delta E = h\nu$$ is absorbed to drive the electron jump. The rest of the light passes through.

Explain the colour you observe**
Your eye never sees the absorbed colour. It sees everything that is left. So the blue colour of copper(II) sulfate solution is the complementary colour to the orange / red / yellow light absorbed. In short: split, promote by absorbing, see the remainder.

Final answer: In $\text{[Cu(H}_{2}\text{O)}_{6}\text{]}^{2+}$ the 3d orbitals are split into two energy levels by the ligands.
An electron is promoted / excited from a lower to a higher 3d orbital.
Energy for this comes from absorption of a specific wavelength / frequency of visible light.
The colour seen is the complementary colour to that absorbed, i.e. the wavelengths not absorbed are transmitted / reflected and seen.

hints: Work out the electron configuration of $\text{Cu}^{+}$ from $\text{Cu}$ ($\text{[Ar]3d}^{10}\text{4s}^{1}$) and think about whether a d electron has anywhere empty to jump to.
walkthrough:
Check the d shell filling**
Copper atom is $\text{[Ar]3d}^{10}\text{4s}^{1}$. Remove the $4\text{s}$ electron to make $\text{Cu}^{+}$ and you are left with $\text{[Ar]3d}^{10}$. Every 3d orbital is completely full.

Link full shell to white appearance**
A d-d transition needs an electron to move from a lower to a higher 3d orbital, which needs an empty space upstairs. With $3\text{d}^{10}$ there is no vacancy, so no visible light can be absorbed in this way. All wavelengths are reflected, which you see as white.
Final answer: $\text{Cu}^{+}$ is $3\text{d}^{10}$, the 3d subshell is full so no d-d electron transition is possible and no visible light is absorbed.

hints: Write the two half equations as reductions: $\text{Cu}^{2+} + \text{e}^{-} \rightleftharpoons \text{Cu}^{+}$ and $\text{I}_{2} + 2\text{e}^{-} \rightleftharpoons 2\text{I}^{-}$, then look up their $E^{\circ}$ values in the Data Booklet.
Remember the rule that the more positive $E^{\circ}$ species gets reduced, and $E^{\circ}_{cell} = E^{\circ}_{reduced} - E^{\circ}_{oxidised}$. Consider what a negative $E^{\circ}_{cell}$ tells you.
walkthrough:
Pull out the correct standard values**
Always write both as reductions. From the Data Booklet: $$\text{Cu}^{2+} + \text{e}^{-} \rightleftharpoons \text{Cu}^{+} \quad E^{\circ} = +0.15\ \text{V}$$ $$\text{I}_{2} + 2\text{e}^{-} \rightleftharpoons 2\text{I}^{-} \quad E^{\circ} = +0.54\ \text{V}$$

Test the proposed reaction**
You are asking $\text{I}^{-}$ to reduce $\text{Cu}^{2+}$. That would mean $\text{Cu}^{2+}$ is reduced and $\text{I}^{-}$ is oxidised. Calculate: $$E^{\circ}_{cell} = E^{\circ}_{cathode} - E^{\circ}_{anode} = (+0.15) - (+0.54) = -0.39\ \text{V}$$ A negative value means the reaction is not feasible under standard conditions. The more positive system, $\text{I}_{2}/\text{I}^{-}$, stays as written, so $\text{I}_{2}$ oxidises $\text{Cu}^{+}$ to $\text{Cu}^{2+}$, not the reverse.

Final answer: $E^{\circ}(\text{Cu}^{2+}/\text{Cu}^{+}) = +0.15\ \text{V}$ and $E^{\circ}(\text{I}_{2}/\text{I}^{-}) = +0.54\ \text{V}$.
$E^{\circ}_{cell} = 0.15 - 0.54 = -0.39\ \text{V}$, negative so not feasible. $\text{I}_{2}$ is a stronger oxidant than $\text{Cu}^{2+}$, so $\text{I}^{-}$ cannot reduce $\text{Cu}^{2+}$ to $\text{Cu}^{+}$ under standard conditions.

hints: Focus on the $\text{Cu}^{2+} + \text{e}^{-} \rightleftharpoons \text{Cu}^{+}$ equilibrium. If $\text{CuI(s)}$ precipitates, what happens to $[\text{Cu}^{+}]$ in solution and which way does that equilibrium shift?

Recall that removing a product drives the reduction forward, making $\text{Cu}^{2+}$ a stronger oxidant. Think about how its $E$ value must move relative to $+0.54\ \text{V}$ for the reaction to now work.
walkthrough:
See why standard conditions no longer apply**
Standard $E^{\circ}$ assumes all ions at $1.0\ \text{mol dm}^{-3}$. Here $\text{CuI}$ is very insoluble, so as soon as $\text{Cu}^{+}$ forms it precipitates. $[\text{Cu}^{+}]$ drops far below $1.0\ \text{mol dm}^{-3}$.

Apply Le Chatelier to the half cell**
Look at $$\text{Cu}^{2+} + \text{e}^{-} \rightleftharpoons \text{Cu}^{+}$$ Removing $\text{Cu}^{+}$ pulls the equilibrium to the right, strongly favouring reduction of $\text{Cu}^{2+}$. That makes $\text{Cu}^{2+}$ a much stronger oxidant, so its electrode potential $E$ becomes more positive than the standard $+0.15\ \text{V}$.

Compare the new potentials**
The $\text{I}_{2}/\text{I}^{-}$ potential is essentially unchanged, near $+0.54\ \text{V}$. The $\text{Cu}^{2+}/\text{Cu}^{+}$ potential rises above $+0.54\ \text{V}$, so $E_{cell}$ for $\text{I}^{-}$ reducing $\text{Cu}^{2+}$ is now positive and the reaction seen in (a) becomes feasible. This is a classic example of solubility altering oxidising power.

Final answer: Precipitation of $\text{CuI}$ removes $\text{Cu}^{+}$ so $[\text{Cu}^{+}]$ is much less than $1.0\ \text{mol dm}^{-3}$ and the $\text{Cu}^{2+}/\text{Cu}^{+}$ equilibrium shifts to the right.
$E(\text{Cu}^{2+}/\text{Cu}^{+})$ becomes more positive, rising above $E(\text{I}_{2}/\text{I}^{-}) = +0.54\ \text{V}$, so $E_{cell}$ becomes positive and $\text{I}^{-}$ can reduce $\text{Cu}^{2+}$.
